title: The next batch's prompts (Nov 4, evening), and the v6 batch (Nov 3–4)
summary:
**The next batch's prompts (Nov 4, evening).** I read what plan and build runs are sent now, as the runner fills it in a dry run (nothing ran). That covers Setup · Basic's prompt, with the config as you'd saved it at 7:20 pm (8 sources, 5 tech stacks, Haiku out of build), and Setup · Advanced's plan and build stages. I checked what they say against this computer, the four engine repos and the v6 agents' answers.

The prompt holds up for my-3d2dge:

- Every placeholder fills.
- The stage texts do what you decided.
- The planner's review is read and flagged.
- PROGRESS.md is worth having: 15 of 24 Opus xhigh builds in v6 were compacted.

The problems are in what's new. Four of the five tech stacks meet text written for my-3d2dge (STACK-1). And this computer has WebGPU, though the agents are told it doesn't (ENV-4). The new findings are at the top of each severity: tick **Unread only** to see just them. Everything below is the v6 audit as it was.

**Later the same evening** you answered, and the fixes went in: each finding says what was done. Then you installed shardfall's two system packages and left tech-v4 as it is, so nothing from this review is left open.

**The v6 batch.** I went through all 120 runs of prompt v6 (Nov 3, 17:47 to Nov 4, 10:55): 24 plans by Opus 5.5 at max effort, each built four times, by Opus xhigh, Opus medium, Sonnet medium and Haiku medium. I read the goal checks in every transcript. Three helper agents read and tagged all 1,344 exit-interview answers, and a fourth read the 24 planners' replies. I spot-checked their counts against the raw answers. I also loaded all 96 games in headless Chromium. Nothing real was run: the dashboard and runner changes were tested in sandboxes with the fake CLIs, and `runs/` is as it was.

What we learned, in short:

1. **The goal check decided the outcome more than the models did.** 73 of 96 builds never passed it, and Claude Code stopped 64 of them after 9 blocked stops. The last checks mostly asked for things this computer can't show (a real pad, sound heard, a person playing) or for proof the agent's own tests couldn't give, and TASK.md forbade asking anyone else. $544 (22%) of the build spend came after a builder first tried to stop. #22 changed the goal and added the machine file after this batch started, so the next batch is the test of that fix (GOAL-1 to GOAL-3).

2. **The plan is the next lever.**
   - Every builder said the plan is too big, and 77 asked for a must/should/could ranking (PLAN-1).
   - 23 of 25 plans write the plan run's own file names, which 67 builders had to translate (PLAN-2).
   - The title rule pulls two ways: 10 builds re-drew the title, and 2 that kept the plan's were marked down for it (PLAN-3).

3. **Opus xhigh is the builder that finishes.**
   - It met the goal 13 times, against 8 for Opus medium, 2 for Sonnet and 0 for Haiku.
   - It costs $96 per goal met, the lowest of the four (Opus medium $115, Sonnet $138).
   - Haiku stopped after 29 minutes (median) and openly cut features (MODEL-1 to MODEL-3).

| | Opus xhigh | Opus medium | Sonnet medium | Haiku medium |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Goal met | 13 of 24 | 8 of 24 | 2 of 24 | 0 of 24 |
| Stopped by Claude Code | 7 | 15 | 22 | 20, and 4 timed out |
| First tried to stop (median) | 124 min | 75 min | 41 min | 29 min |
| Time (median) | 162 min | 110 min | 56 min | 56 min |
| Cost (median / total) | $54 / $1,253 | $38 / $919 | $10 / $275 | $6 / $147 |
| Cost per goal met | $96 | $115 | $138 | none met |
| Issues its own testing found (median) | 33 | 25 | 10 | 12 |
| Changed the engine | 24 | 24 | 19 | 11 |
| Drew its own title | 1 | 2 | 0 | 7 |
| Game size (median) | 1,746 KB | 1,641 KB | 1,467 KB | 1,425 KB |
| Attract demo starts on its own (within 2 min) | 24 | 24 | 23 (1 throws on every frame) | 23 (1 throws on every frame) |
| No touch-only notice | 0 | 0 | 2 | 3 |

4. **Run data had a hole.** None of the 64 builds Claude Code stopped kept its final reply: the CLI's result was empty, though the answer was in the output. The runner now reads it, and `--reparse` fills the 64 in. That rewrites committed run data, so the permission check stopped me, and it's your call (DATA-1).

5. **The computer was under strain.**
   - All 24 planners filled /tmp, which is held in memory, by downloading the engine and hub repos into it at the same time. 6.4 GB of older agent leftovers are still there.
   - 33 test servers that agents started are still running (ENV-1, ENV-2).

6. **The games mostly hold up when loaded cold.** All 96 load headless without an error. Two attract modes throw on every frame, and 5 games skip the touch-only notice, though their builders' tests passed (GAME-1).

The Insights tab gained **What the agents said**, which shows every answer to one question across the runs in view, by model, with a search. It also has a check that the builds of one plan keep its title. Engine feedback for the my-3D2dge repo is under Engine.

**Since then (Nov 4, later):**

- The 64 lost replies are back, and the 378 older games carry their record.
- /tmp and the stray servers are cleaned up.
- Builders draw their own titles, and Usage is added on import.
- The runner gives each run its own temp folder, stops what an agent leaves running, and loads every finished game headless for a minute (the game check).
- Haiku stays in the dashboard but won't be a primary builder. At this plan size it pays its higher price on 93% of calls, so a build costs half of a Sonnet build, and it met no goals (MODEL-1).

The v6 audit left three decisions under Your call.

decisions.title: Check the finished games: `node run-matrix.mjs --check-games` (GAME-1)
decisions.detail: New runs get the game check as they end. This command checks the games already in `runs/` that haven't been checked: about 70 s per game, two at a time. That's about an hour for the 96 v6 games and about 4 hours for all 470 or so. It writes `gameCheck` into each result.json and a `game-check.png` beside it. It never touches the game files.

decisions.title: Keep file names out of PLAN.md (PLAN-2)
decisions.detail: Optional. The planner copies its own file names into the plan, and every builder has to translate them. It cost time but caused no wrong files. Now that builders draw their own titles, the plan's names will match even less. A line in the plan stage would do it: "Write paths relative to the dev folder; each builder takes its own file names from its TASK.md."

decisions.title: Watch the goal check in the next batch (GOAL-3)
decisions.detail: If builders still get blocked for lacking an "independent" review, either allow one review subagent at the end, or say in the goal that the agent's own tests count.

findings.title: Four of the five tech stacks get testing, art and engine text written for my-3d2dge
findings.found:
Tech Stack now has five variants: my-3d2dge-v3, shardfall, riftlight, my-3dge and tech-v4. Other sections still assume my-3d2dge:

- **Testing** says to test with "the engine's game.advance and game.debug, as in game/test.mjs". Only my-3d2dge has those: I listed all four repos' files, and `game/test.mjs` is only in my-3d2dge. The others test their own way. shardfall uses `cargo test` and its own tools, riftlight uses vitest and `npm run look`, and my-3dge uses its workspace's checks.
- **Art Direction, Animation and Working Environment** say "the engine's native style", "the engine's native animation system" and "the engine's headless tools". tech-v4 (Three.js R180 and Rapier) has no engine, so these have nothing to point at, and neither do Engine Feedback's six questions about "the engine".
- **Where they start.** my-3d2dge's variant points at its agent handoff (`dist/handoff`). The other three point at the repo root, though each has its own way in for agents: shardfall's `START_HERE.md` and `docs/MAKE_A_GAME.md`, riftlight's engine kit (`npm run bundle`, with `docs/GUIDE.md`), and my-3dge's `lean/README.md` or its README's "Make a game with my-3dge".
- **my-3dge's engine is pinned.** Its new-game script copies the engine in read-only, pinned by `engine-lock.json`. The variant says "You may change anything in it, the engine included".
findings.did:
**Done Nov 4**, after your answers:

- **Testing:** you took the engine's names out (`test-tools-v2`).
- **Where they start:** each engine's own way in for agents.
  - shardfall: `https://github.com/michaelcrosato/shardfall/blob/main/START_HERE.md`. Its route for a new game is docs/MAKE_A_GAME.md.
  - riftlight: the engine kit, `https://github.com/michaelcrosato/riftlight/releases/latest/download/pixel-engine.zip`.
  - my-3dge: its full workspace, `https://github.com/michaelcrosato/my-3dge#make-a-game-with-my-3dge`, the route its handoff gives a coding agent that tests headless.
- **Changing the engine:**
  - riftlight and my-3dge now say to keep the engine as it ships and add whatever the game needs on top of it, as their own guides say. riftlight's: "Never edit pixel-engine.js". my-3dge's: the engine is read-only, `npm run check` fails when it changes, and a patch is only for when there's no workaround, listed in its ENGINE-FEEDBACK.md.
  - So yes, the agent can still build whatever it wants, on top. Both export three.js and Rapier to the game's own code.
  - shardfall keeps "You may change anything in it, the engine included". A game compiles into its engine crate, and its guide says menus and new sounds need engine code.
- The pinned copies of the three variants got the same text. None of them had run, so they kept their names.

tech-v4 has no engine, so Art and Animation's "the engine's native style" has nothing to point at. **Your call (Nov 4): leave it as it is.**
findings.check: Read each engine's handoff: shardfall's START_HERE.md and MAKE_A_GAME.md, riftlight's README, kit README and GUIDE.md, and my-3dge's HANDOFF.md, README and the AGENTS.md template its new-game script writes.

findings.title: This computer has WebGPU in Chromium with one flag, but the agents are told it has none, and the game check doesn't use it
findings.found:
Four of the five stacks draw with WebGPU: shardfall (wgpu), riftlight ("WebGPU-first", three/webgpu), my-3dge ("WebGPU only") and tech-v4 ("WEBGPU").

- **The machine file says "no WebGPU".** check-environment.mjs looks for `navigator.gpu` on a blank page. A blank page isn't a secure context, so WebGPU is never there, whatever the browser can do.
- **What's true:** on a `file://` page, Chromium 153 gets a WebGPU adapter (SwiftShader, in software) when it's started with `--enable-unsafe-webgpu`. Without the flag, `requestAdapter()` returns nothing. Firefox 155 and WebKit 26.6 have no WebGPU at all. my-3dge's README says the same: "Chromium 153 (WebGPU on SwiftShader)".
- **The game check** (check-game.py) starts Chromium without the flag. A WebGPU-only game gets no adapter there, so the check sees its no-WebGPU path, not the game.
findings.did:
**Done Nov 4.** `check-game.py` now starts Chromium with `--enable-unsafe-webgpu --enable-features=Vulkan --use-webgpu-adapter=swiftshader`.

- `--enable-unsafe-webgpu` alone found an adapter, but shardfall's device was lost as it started ("Device was destroyed").
- Adding `--use-vulkan=swiftshader` made a v6 WebGL game's screenshot time out (30 s).
- With the three flags, shardfall's, riftlight's and my-3dge's games start with no errors. Before, each failed with "no WebGPU". A v6 WebGL game's check came out the same as before.
- riftlight's title screen shows in the screenshot. shardfall's and my-3dge's canvases came out white, though their logs and HUD show them running. A WebGPU canvas drawing about a frame a second in software can miss the screenshot, so its errors are what count. That's in the README and the machine file.

`check-environment.mjs` now probes on a `file://` page, and asks Chromium again with those flags. `environments/Worki9.md` now says Chromium has WebGPU with them, on `file://` or `http://127.0.0.1` pages, in software.
findings.check: Ran the old and new check-game.py on shardfall's starter (built here), riftlight's latest single-file build, my-3dge's lean example and a v6 WebGL game, and tried six flag sets on the WebGPU ones.

findings.title: 73 of 96 builds never passed their goal check; Claude Code stopped 64 of them after 9 blocked stops
findings.found:
Goal met: Opus xhigh 13 of 24, Opus medium 8, Sonnet 2, Haiku 0. All 24 plans passed on the first check. 17 of 24 briefs had at least one build that passed.

The last check of each unmet build said what was missing. I read all 73:

- **Things this computer can't show.** No physical DualSense, no touch device, sound never heard, no human playthrough, no real AI Hub session with people. These come up in most Opus and Sonnet failures. Example: sonnet-medium TimeCrisis3 was checked 48 times in 32 minutes on the same three items: "Real DualSense: there is no physical controller", boss-state replica sync and one death never seen on screen.
- **The agent's own evidence wasn't independent enough** (GOAL-3).
- **Features really missing**, mostly Haiku. For example, haiku-medium WipeoutHD had "only 5 of 10 weapons, 2 of 4 tracks". 4 Haiku runs stopped to ask the user to choose a narrower scope, which nobody can answer in a headless run (densha-de-go, tenchu2, TrackMania and brigandine).
- **Reply format.** 4 Sonnet runs said the sections were "in my previous reply" instead of repeating them.
- **The title** (PLAN-3).
findings.did:
Nothing new here: #22 (merged today, after this batch started) is the fix.

- It changed the build goal to "Everything in PLAN.md that can be done on this computer is done, and everything TASK.md asks you to hand in is in this folder."
- It added `environments/Worki9.md`. That file says what this computer can't test, gives the stand-ins to use, and says anything that needs the real thing "is checked as far as it can be here, never required".

The next batch is the test. Insights → Expectations → "Finished runs meet their /goal" shows the rate.
findings.check: `goalMet`, `goalChecks`, `goalForced` and `goalReason` in all 120 result.json files, and each check read again from the transcripts in `~/.claude/projects` (117 of 120 found; 3 Haiku runs that hit the time limit have none).

findings.title: 64 builds had no final reply: Claude Code's result is empty when it stops a /goal turn itself
findings.found:
When Claude Code overrides the stop hook after 9 blocks, the stream's last `result` line has `"result":""`. The runner took the reply only from that line, so `reply.md` was never written. Results' reply button and the record in each game came up empty for these runs, and Insights flagged them under "no reply" (77 of 488 finished runs).

The answer isn't lost. The agent's last response in `agent.out` holds it. In sonnet-medium TimeCrisis3 it has all four sections. Affected builds: Haiku 20, Sonnet 22, Opus medium 15, Opus xhigh 7. Older forced runs from Nov 3 are affected too.
findings.did:
`parseClaude` now falls back to the last response's text when the result is empty (not for an error, and not for a made-up `<synthetic>` message), as `sessionEnd` already did for runs cut off mid-session. `--reparse` now writes `reply.md` for a run that has none and whose output has a reply; a `reply.md` already there is left alone. Running it on the real runs is in Your call.

**Done Nov 4:** you ran `--reparse`, and the 64 builds plus 4 older stopped runs got their `reply.md`. One more case came up: the Haiku Wiretap build was resumed three times, and its `reply.md` held the first sessions' "Credit balance is too low". I wrote in its real final reply. `--reparse` now does that itself: a reply.md holding an earlier session's reply gives way to the last session's. The resume test covers it.
findings.check: `test/runner.test.mjs` (the /goal test): the fake Claude CLI now ends a forced turn with an empty result like the real one. The reply comes from the last response, and `--reparse` fills in a deleted `reply.md` and leaves one that's there alone. The test fails on the old runner. A sandbox copy of 5 real runs (3 forced) gave the 3 forced runs their reply (1,783 to 4,309 characters) and changed nothing else.

findings.title: Every builder said the plan was bigger than one session, and 77 asked for it to be ranked
findings.found:
The plans run 113 to 201 KB (median 142 KB, about 1,500 to 2,400 lines). They cover 8 to 14 milestones and 10 to 16 risks, with several modes, tracks or chapters each. All 96 builders raised scope somewhere in their prompt feedback: opus-xhigh 3, opus-medium 13, Sonnet 24 and Haiku 21 called it confusing or too big.

Their most common request was "rank the plan must/should/could, with a cut order" (77 runs). Next came a time or token budget (19), a smaller first milestone (18) and a target size for the demo (13).

The "done" bar read as the whole plan in 27 runs. Done and the goal say "every feature … no stubs", and STAGE.md says to follow the plan, so nothing could be left out without counting as a stub. opus-medium american-football: "'follow the plan' versus 'TASK.md wins' and 'no stubbed features' needed judgment about what to cut without leaving stubs".

How long each builder worked before it first tried to stop (median): Haiku 29 minutes, Sonnet 41, Opus medium 75, Opus xhigh 124.
findings.did: **Decided: no ranking.** The plan stays the whole design, and the goal-met rate measures how much of it each builder finishes. Note that #22's build goal is "everything in PLAN.md that can be done on this computer is done", so the bar is still the whole plan.
findings.check: The prompt-feedback catalogue (all 384 answers tagged; every quote checked to be verbatim), PLAN.md sizes from `planChars`, and first-check times from the transcripts.

findings.title: All 24 planners filled /tmp, which is held in memory, and 6.4 GB of older agent work is still in it
findings.found:
/tmp is a 9.8 GB tmpfs, so whatever sits in it uses RAM on a computer with 20 GB.

- **During the batch:** all 24 plan transcripts hit "No space left on device" or Claude Code's "0 MB free" notice, and so did 19 of 93 build transcripts. 22 of 24 planners downloaded the engine and ai-hub repos into /tmp, all starting within about a minute of each other. Three plans lost command output to it. The planners blamed "other agents".
- **Now:** 1.8 GB is free. 6.4 GB is older agent work, mostly `/tmp/bb-xb81546/dl` (5.4 GB, from the Nov 2 Breaking Bad runs). The rest is `/tmp/x22cc1b-dl`, `/tmp/s55eng`, `/tmp/mm-research-xe8b2f0`, `/tmp/x3ec78e`, `/tmp/s55` and `/tmp/x96eb17`, each 150 to 175 MB.
- **During this audit:** a sandbox copy of mine filled it for a moment. I deleted it at once and moved my sandboxes to `~/.cache`.
findings.did: **Done Nov 4:** you deleted the old /tmp folders; /tmp went from 7.8 GB used to 1.4 GB. Each run now gets a temp folder of its own, `tmp/` beside `work/` (`TMPDIR`, `TMP`, `TEMP` and `CLAUDE_CODE_TMPDIR`), so tools that write temp files can't fill /tmp. Agents that write to /tmp by name still can; the machine file asks them not to.
findings.check: `df -h /tmp`, `du -sh /tmp/*`, and a search of all 117 transcripts for the full-disk messages and for downloads into /tmp.

findings.title: Builders made the same engine patches up to 55 times over, so they belong in my-3D2dge
findings.found:
78 of 96 builds changed the engine: all 48 Opus builds, 19 Sonnet and 11 Haiku. The same changes were made over and over, each copy on its own:

| Change | Runs |
|---|---|
| PlayStation button symbols by default (the setting defaults to "auto", and a game can't set it) | 55 |
| A public audio bus, so code-made voices follow volume and mute | 39 |
| Font glyphs: the 5×7 pixel font has no ✕ ○ □ △, though `input.label()` returns them, so they print as "?" (55 runs hit this); also missing are the middle dot, dashes, arrows, ticks and accents | 32 |
| A per-letter voice hook in E.Dialog (it plays one sound per page) | 29 |
| A guard so the AI Hub's Create+Options doesn't open the pause menu | 22 |
| Humanoid hats and hair, outfits, weapons | 19, 17, 16 |
| Settings rows on any Shell screen; synth extensions | 11 each |
| Analog triggers; an exported per-step hook | 8 each |

TASK.md requires PlayStation symbols by default, so the first row is a patch every game needs. The plans asked for several of these patches up front.
findings.did: Nothing here: it's for the engine repo. Each run's own patch is in its dev folder, under `runs/<run>/work/<Game>/` (not in git). The Engine Feedback question in Insights → What the agents said has every answer.
findings.check: Engine-feedback catalogue: all 576 answers tagged; every quote checked to be verbatim, and every run key checked to exist. I spot-checked the button-symbol, audio-bus and font counts against the raw answers (61, 37 and 32 mentions).

findings.title: shardfall's one-page build needs wasm-bindgen-cli 0.2.129, which this computer doesn't have
findings.found:
shardfall makes its single-file game with `scripts/build-web.sh --single-file`. That needs two things:

- **The wasm32 target** for the Rust it pins (1.98.1). It's already installed here.
- **wasm-bindgen** at the version in its Cargo.lock (0.2.129). It isn't installed.

So each shardfall builder would `cargo install` it into the shared `~/.cargo/bin`, outside its folder, several at a time. As saved, there are up to 24 shardfall builds (8 sources × 3 builders). They would also compile wgpu and Rapier in release mode side by side, on 20 GB of RAM.
findings.did:
**Done Nov 4:**

- Installed `wasm-bindgen-cli` 0.2.129 (`~/.cargo/bin`).
- A test build in a throwaway clone made shardfall's starter as one page (11.4 MB, 1 min 18 s).
- The machine file lists `wasm-bindgen 0.2.129`, plus a Rust line: the toolchains, and which have the wasm32 target (1.98.1, the one shardfall pins).

**Then you installed the two packages** (`libasound2-dev`, `libudev-dev`), and shardfall's headless tool works here. In a throwaway clone (Nov 4), `pav` built in 1 min 23 s. The starter's bot won 3 of 3 seeds (`pav play scene=starter bot=true seeds=3`), and `pav capture` drew the starter at 640×360 in software.

The home computer needs the same three steps: `sudo apt-get install -y libasound2-dev libudev-dev`, `cargo install wasm-bindgen-cli --version 0.2.129`, and `rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown --toolchain 1.98.1`.
findings.check: `cargo build -p pav_tools --bin pav` stopped at alsa-sys ("pkg-config … alsa"); `pkg-config --exists alsa libudev` both fail; `sudo -n true` asks for a password.

findings.title: The machine file's uv tip hides Playwright, and the obvious fix asks for `playwright install`
findings.found:
The machine file says "The system Python has no packages installed. For one (Pillow, numpy …), use uv: `uv run --with pillow python script.py`". But Python's Playwright 1.63 is installed (in `~/.local`), and the same file tells agents to use it.

- `uv run --with pillow` runs in its own environment, so `import playwright` fails there (ModuleNotFoundError).
- Adding `--with playwright` gets the newest version, 1.64.1. It can't find the browsers downloaded for 1.63, and it says to run `playwright install`, which the same section forbids.
- `--with playwright==1.63.0` works with the browsers already here.

Any script that screenshots the game and reads the pixels with Pillow hits this. No run has yet: the v6 batch ran before this file existed. This line was also added to Worki9.md by hand. It isn't in check-environment.mjs's starting text, so another computer's file won't have it.
findings.did: **Done Nov 4.** The line in Worki9.md now says the system Python has Playwright and nothing else. For other packages, use `uv run --with pillow python script.py`, adding `--with playwright==1.63.0` when the script drives a browser too. `check-environment.mjs` writes the same line, with this computer's Playwright version, into a new computer's file.
findings.check: Ran a Pillow + Playwright script under uv three ways: without Playwright, with the newest Playwright, and with 1.63.0.

findings.title: Agents are told to keep their files in their own folder, so a plan's research clones may now reach every build
findings.found:
In v6, 22 of 24 planners downloaded the engine and ai-hub repos into /tmp (ENV-1), and every plan's work folder held only PLAN.md, STAGE.md and TASK.md (ENV-3). The machine file now says "Keep every file you make inside your own folder, not /tmp or a parent folder". A planner that follows it puts its clones in `work/`. A build starts from a copy of its plan's `work/` (without node_modules and .git), so the plan's research copies (about 20 to 175 MB each in v6) would go to all three of its builds.

The runner already gives each run a temp folder for this: `tmp/` beside `work/`, as $TMPDIR, which later stages don't get. But:

- The prompt never mentions it, and by the prompt's own words it's "a parent folder".
- Nothing deletes `tmp/` when a run ends. Under "commit everything in runs/", its clones would go into git with their .git folders (the broken-gitlink problem).
findings.did:
**Done Nov 4**, your way: the prompt doesn't mention it, and the runner cleans up.

- Each run's `tmp/` is deleted once the run has finished, OK or failed, after what its agent left running is stopped and its game is checked.
- A cut-off run keeps it, to carry on with.
- `runs/*/tmp/` is in `.gitignore`, for runs still going when you commit.

A planner that clones the engine into `work/` still passes the clone on to its builds. You said space isn't an issue, so that's left as it is.
findings.check: Read prepareStage and agentEnv in run-matrix.mjs, and the machine file as it's sent.

findings.title: Changing a stage's text doesn't make its runs run again, and nothing warns you
findings.found:
A stage run is matched by its chain (each step's stage, model and effort) and its brief (one variant per dimension). The stage's Instructions and Done when aren't part of that, and result.json keeps no hash of them. So after you edit a stage's text, its finished runs still count as done, and the new text never runs for those briefs.

- **No warning.** Setup warns about this for an edited variant ("…used its earlier text"), but not for a stage.
- **Results can't tell them apart.** Within one prompt version, a run of the old text and a run of the new one look the same.

The next batch isn't affected. Its brief is new (new sources, Source Information v3), so 0 of its 160 runs count as done.
findings.did:
**Done Nov 4.** Stages follow the variants' convention now:

- **What's saved:** each stage run records `stageHashes`, a hash of its stage's text and goal as set.
- **What shows:** Results marks a run whose stage was edited since ("old text"), and Insights and the Run tab count it like an edited variant. Setup warns about a stage edited outside the page while it has runs. Runs from before this are checked against their `prompt.md` and `goal.md`.
- **Names follow the text:** editing a stage that has runs, in Setup · Advanced, renames it as you type (`plan` → `plan-v2`), with a note under it. Putting the old text back brings the old name back, and a name typed by hand stays.
- Stage names may have a hyphen now.

**The current stages:** the 25 plans and 100 builds of Nov 3–4 all used the old texts, so today's plan and build texts have never run. They're now `plan-v2` and `build-v2`, so their runs don't count as the old ones'. Their folders are named `….plan-v2__…` and `….build-v2__…`.
findings.check: Read runKey, chainKey and stageRuns in run-matrix.mjs, and validate() in the dashboard. Also did a dry run of the config as saved.

findings.title: After the first stop attempt, the medium builders mostly just tried to stop again
findings.found:
Most builds that kept going after a failed check didn't do much new work. They mostly ran the tests again and wrote the same message again.

| | Haiku | Sonnet | Opus medium | Opus xhigh |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Re-checks within a minute of the one before | 76% | 83% | 65% | 55% |
| Median gap between checks | 0.1 min | 0.2 min | 0.4 min | 4.6 min |

findings.title: The scripted playthrough is the most useful test, but headless runs that skip drawing hid real bugs
findings.found:
What the builders said about their own tests (testing catalogue, 96 runs):

- **Most helpful:** a scripted bot playthrough of the whole game (72). Next came AI-against-AI simulations (15) and the AI Hub harness (6 as the top pick, 19 mentions).
- **Least helpful:** screenshots (19), smoke checks (16), determinism checks that "never failed" (14), and unit or data checks that never failed (12).

**Screenshots found more than they got credit for.** In the 19 runs that say where each issue was found, screenshots found 236 of 621 issues (38%). Some crashes were caught only that way: haiku-medium BigBuckHunterPro's crash was "found by a screenshot … not by the Node tests, which had passed".

**Headless Node runs skip drawing, so:**

- Draw-time crashes passed the suites in 6 runs.
- Menus whose hit areas exist only after a draw broke scripted input in 9.
- Esc and pause clashed with Dev mode, or unbound keys didn't end the attract mode, in 12 Opus runs.

Determinism checks never failed, yet 10 runs report Math.random leaks or replay drift.

"Critical" is used loosely. Runs count 12 fps rendering, slow AI turns and camera framing as critical, so the Q2 numbers don't compare well across builders.

findings.title: 38 specific engine bugs that builders described, 15 of them found only by Opus xhigh
findings.found:
Reported by the builders (I didn't reproduce them):

- **Input**
  - A scripted tap sets the last device to touch.
  - `halfKeys` gives two menu actions the same key.
  - Pad codes are released every tick when no pad is connected.
  - `feed('move')` doesn't update `mouse.t`, which menus use for hover.
  - `Input.use()` drops held keys.
  - A tap releases a hold on the same action.
- **Rigs**
  - `rig.update` with `vx` but no `vy` gives a permanent NaN walk phase.
  - `Math.random` in the constructor and in blinking breaks determinism.
- **Views**
  - E.View rounding puts rigs up to 7 px off their hit zones.
  - Sprites scale by zoom alone, while geometry scales by view scale × zoom.
  - `m7.shape` ignores params and mats.
  - E.Road projects x and y with different scales, which squashes wide screens.
  - The x-ray mask uses a fixed box per item.
  - Depth sorting breaks for big geometry.
  - The chunked floor-cache trim was broken.
- **3D add-on**
  - With the cel filter on, the first-person overlay renders black.
  - Post filters render black without a GPU.
  - A literal `</script>` in the header breaks single-file builds.
  - Split-screen viewports are numbered from the bottom.
  - Text planes come out mirrored.
- **Other**
  - The 0.15 s music look-ahead drops notes on laggy outputs such as Bluetooth.
  - E.Arcade reads only player one.
  - A hit-stop timer leaves `timeScale` changed across scenes.
  - FlowField keeps the old map and ignores `map.solid`.
  - E.hex returns arrays that the px helpers reject.

Silent failures come up again and again: rgb() colours draw magenta, a scene field named `view` is replaced, a `camera()` method overrides the option, and mocap clips never play. Undocumented argument orders and return shapes cost 36 runs; for example, `mouseGround` returns `[x, y]`, which made a camera NaN.

TV readability (36 runs): E.Menu is fixed at scale 1 with no scrolling, the HTML Shell uses 14 px text, and E.Dialog has no width option.

findings.title: All 96 games start headless without an error; 2 attract modes throw on every frame, and 5 games miss the touch notice
findings.found:
I loaded each game's .html from `file://` in headless Chromium (software WebGL), first at 1280×720 and then on a 390×844 touch phone. No input for 16 seconds, then Enter twice.

- **Loading:** all 96 loaded in under 2.5 s, with no uncaught errors, and every CDN library loaded.
- **Attract modes that throw on every frame.** The engine catches it and logs `error in draw (scene "attract")`. Neither builder's tests caught it.
  - haiku-medium basketball (Zonefire): "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'sky')" in `drawCourt`. The error text also shows on screen.
  - sonnet-medium brigandine (Brigantime): "Cannot set properties of null (setting 'stage')".
- **No title screen:** haiku-medium TrackMania (Crackmania) opens straight into a tutorial dialog over an empty sky, with no title or menu, and stays there through Enter.
- **Attract mode:** with no input, 94 of 96 started an attract demo within 2 minutes. Only 47 had by 26 s and 86 by 60 s, because the games ran at 6 to 60 fps here (median 19, in software rendering), and a game whose clock advances per frame counts its 10 seconds slowly. The two that never start are the Sonnet and Haiku TrackMania builds: their opening dialog waits for a key.
- **The touch-only notice** ("Controller or keyboard required" and Settings) shows on 87 of 96.
  - It's missing in haiku-medium DOAX, Eye of the Beholder and TrackMania, and in sonnet-medium WipeoutHD and densha-de-go.
  - Two Operation Wolf builds draw their whole screen as a small 16:9 box on a portrait phone, too small to tell.
  - Two 3D builds were still showing the engine's boot log at 4.5 s.
  - In about 10 games the notice text runs off the sides of a portrait screen.
- **Enter:** it changed the screen in 95 of 96.
findings.did:
The runner now does this for every new game. With `gameCheck` in the config, it loads each finished game in headless Chromium for 60 s and records what it throws, logs or fails to load, with a screenshot. Needs a look flags a game with errors, its details show the check, and Expectations counts them. `node run-matrix.mjs --check-games` checks the runs that finished before (see Your call).

Zonefire's attract error showed up in 4 of 4 loads from its run folder, but in none from a copy elsewhere. The page asks for nothing else, so it likely picks something at random from its own path, and some picks crash.
findings.check: Playwright (Chromium 153, software WebGL). Screenshots at 4, 14, 16 and 26 s, after Enter and on the touch phone, then at 60 and 120 s for the games still on their title, with their frame rate measured. All reviewed by eye on contact sheets, with console and page errors recorded throughout. This shows what loads and runs on its own, not whether a game is good: nothing was played.

findings.check: `node run-matrix.mjs --dry-run --json --stages`, which starts nothing, and v6's costUsd.

findings.title: Insights: What the agents said, every answer to one question side by side
findings.found: Each exit interview could only be read one run at a time, from the interview button in Results. Comparing 96 answers to "What was confusing?" meant opening 96 files.
findings.did:
A new Insights card for the runs in view:

- Pick a question to read every answer to it, by model + effort.
- **Search** finds a word in all answers, and the question list then shows how many answers have it.
- **Copy** puts the answers shown on the clipboard as plain text, for pasting into a document or a chat.

Answers come from `/api/feedback`. That's each exit interview's lists paired with the questions the run was sent, from the config, the prompt as sent or the record in the game. It also includes the planners' reviews (`plannerAnswers`).
findings.check: Sandbox dashboard with the real run records and fake CLIs: the answers of 124 runs, all but 2 paired with their questions (26 older runs through their game's record). It renders in Chromium at 1366 px and WebKit at 390 px with no console errors and no sideways scroll. The search found 4 of 122 answers to "What was confusing?" with "attract". `node --test` passes.

findings.title: Insights: the check that a plan's builds share its title, added and then taken out
findings.found: Nothing showed when a plan's builds came out under different names (PLAN-3).
findings.did: Taken out when you decided that builders draw their own titles (PLAN-3): different titles are now the plan.
findings.check: The sandbox dashboard lists Sublime Crisis 3 / Tide Crisis 3, Dipout HD / Snipeout HD, and Operation Wolfpack / Operation Big Bad Wolf, the same mismatches I found by script.

changes.title: WebGPU in the game check and the machine file
changes.detail: `check-game.py` starts Chromium with `--enable-unsafe-webgpu --enable-features=Vulkan --use-webgpu-adapter=swiftshader`, so WebGPU games run there in software. `check-environment.mjs` probes on a `file://` page and says which flags WebGPU needs (ENV-4).

changes.title: Each engine starts at its own handoff
changes.detail: shardfall: START_HERE.md. riftlight: its engine kit. my-3dge: its full workspace. riftlight and my-3dge keep their engine as it ships and build on top (STACK-1).

changes.title: wasm-bindgen for shardfall, and Rust in the machine file
changes.detail: wasm-bindgen-cli 0.2.129 is installed here. The machine file lists it, and Rust's toolchains with the wasm32 target (ENV-5). The uv line pins Playwright 1.63.0 (ENV-6).

changes.title: Stage names follow their text
changes.detail: Stage runs record `stageHashes`. Editing a stage that has runs renames it (`plan` → `plan-v2`), Results marks runs of an earlier text, and Setup warns. Today's stages are `plan-v2` and `build-v2` (DASH-3).

changes.title: A run's temp folder goes once it's done
changes.detail: `tmp/` is deleted when a run finishes (a cut-off run keeps it), and `runs/*/tmp/` is in `.gitignore` (ENV-7).

changes.title: Prompt fixes
changes.detail: `ws-sub-v3` (folders beside this one), `pkg-html-v3` (file name brackets), `on-exit-v2` ("that can be done on this computer"). Also the machine file's headings a level down, no "browser unknown", no trailing spaces, the current ready-made stages, and the README (PROMPT-4, PROMPT-5, GOAL-4, DASH-4).

changes.title: Replies of /goal runs Claude Code stopped
changes.detail: The runner takes the agent's last response when the CLI's result is empty, and `--reparse` fills in a missing `reply.md` (DATA-1).

changes.title: Stamping again only rewrites changed games
changes.detail: `--reparse` and `--stamp` leave a game whose record would only get a new `stampedAt` (DATA-2).

changes.title: What the agents said (Insights)
changes.detail: Every answer to one exit-interview or planner-review question across the runs in view, by model + effort, with a search and Copy (DASH-1).

changes.title: Goal checks with no verdict show as unknown
Audit tab: a little Markdown
changes.detail: **Bold**, lists (with one level of sub-items) and simple tables render in an audit's text, which this audit's tables need. Plain text renders as before.

changes.title: The Insights card waits for a restart
changes.detail: A dashboard started before this change has no `/api/feedback`, so the card asks for a restart (Run tab → ⟳ Restart dashboard) instead of showing nothing (`canFeedback`, like `canResume`).

changes.title: README
changes.detail: The new card and check, how the reply is read, what `--reparse` now fills in, stamping only changed games, and the Audit tab's Markdown.

changes.title: The game check
changes.detail: With `gameCheck` in the config (on, 60 s), the runner loads each finished game headless and records its errors and a screenshot (`check-game.py`; Needs a look, details, Expectations). `--check-games` for older runs.

changes.title: A temp folder per run, and leftovers stopped
changes.detail: `tmp/` beside `work/` is each run's TMPDIR. Processes an agent leaves running in its folder are stopped when it exits (`leftovers`).

changes.title: Builders draw their own titles
changes.detail: The plan stage leaves the title to the builders. The Insights title check is gone.

changes.title: Usage is added on import
changes.detail: `info-exit-v3`: the agent writes "added on import", and the exit interview names the fields that come from the run's record later.

changes.title: Smaller follow-ups
changes.detail: A resumed run's stale reply.md gives way on `--reparse`. The flaky resume test waits 5 s, so it no longer races (4 of 4 at once pass). The 378 older games have their record stamped in (schema 2).

tests.summary: The Nov 4 evening fixes, tested against fake CLIs in throwaway folders; `runs/` wasn't touched. The game check's flags were also tried on real games: shardfall, riftlight, my-3dge and a v6 WebGL game.

suites.name: `node --test test/*.test.mjs`
suites.detail:
Runner, server, record and environment tests. New or changed:

- A stage name with a hyphen, and the stage hashes a run records.
- A run's temp folder deleted once it's done, and kept by a cut-off run until it carries on.
- The machine file's headings a level down.
- The server marking a run whose stage was edited since, by its hashes or, for an older run, by what it was sent, and the stage texts runs used.

suites.name: `python3 test/ui_check.py`
suites.detail: Every tab at five sizes in Chromium, WebKit and Firefox, and the live checks. New: editing a stage that ran renames it to plan-v2 with a note, typing keeps focus, and the old text brings the old name back.

screens.summary: `viewport-matrix` on the Insights tab with the new **What the agents said** card, served by a sandbox dashboard with the real run records (fake CLIs, nothing real could run): iPhones and iPads in WebKit, Android in Chromium, desktop sizes in all three engines. None scrolls sideways or logs a console error. `test/ui_check.py` covers every other tab.
